content: 1. Stool specimen collection must be conducted properly, ensuring that the first and second samples are collected at least 24 hours apart. If caregivers are responsible for collecting stool specimens, they must be provided with clear instructions to ensure proper collection. 2. Inadequate stool specimens or the death of a case can hinder the investigation process. It is essential to ensure that stool specimens are collected in a timely and adequate manner. 3. Cases may become untraceable due to discharge, travel, or other reasons. It is critical to maintain accurate and up-to-date contact information and addresses for all cases to facilitate follow-up. 4. Case investigation kits must be readily available to ensure timely and effective investigations. 5. In situations where stool specimens are inadequate, clear instructions must be provided to nurses and caregivers on how to collect contact samples properly. 6. Specimen transport must be planned in advance, including contingency plans for alternative routes or carriers in case of road closures, lockdowns, or other disruptions. 7. Special permissions for sample transport should be obtained if necessary, and alternative WHO-accredited laboratories should be identified for processing samples when required. 8. Specimens should not be batched unnecessarily, as this can delay processing. Priority should be given to shipping samples from suspected hot cases immediately. 9. Both stool specimens must arrive at the laboratory within three days of the second specimen's collection to ensure timely analysis. 10. Poor planning for transport, road closures, insecurity, or international border restrictions can delay sample shipment. Contingency plans, such as using humanitarian flights or alternative laboratories, should be in place to address these challenges. 11. A minimum buffer stock of critical consumables and reagents sufficient for a one-year workload should be maintained when placing orders to avoid disruptions in laboratory operations. 12. Shipping contracts with multiple in-country couriers should be secured to ensure reliable transport of specimens. 13. Surveillance indicators, such as stool adequacy, timeliness of collection, and condition of specimens upon arrival, must meet the target of at least 80% to ensure effective monitoring of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) cases. 14. Community-based surveillance (CBS) should aim to report a high proportion of AFP cases, with completeness and timeliness of weekly or monthly zero reporting (WZR/MZR) exceeding 80%. 15. Gender-related barriers, such as limited decision-making power, mobility restrictions, and lack of awareness among women caregivers, must be addressed to improve care-seeking behavior and timely notification of AFP cases. 16. Gender-sensitive and gender-responsive approaches should be integrated into all health interventions to address inequalities and ensure equitable access to healthcare services. 17. Gender-transformative strategies should aim to redefine and change existing gender roles, norms, and practices to tackle the root causes of gender inequality and reshape power dynamics. 18. Surveillance systems must identify and address gender-related delays in case detection and notification, particularly in high-risk areas and among special populations. 19. Female health workers and community informants should receive adequate training, supervision, and support to enhance their capacity to identify and report AFP cases effectively. 20. Gender analysis and community sensitization activities should involve men and address local barriers to healthcare access, such as transportation, financial constraints, and cultural norms. 21. Surveillance networks must ensure that AFP cases are detected and reported promptly, with a focus on improving the appropriateness and completeness of health encounter information. 22. Indicators related to health-seeking behaviors, such as the proportion of AFP cases with timely health encounters and adequacy of notification by reporting sources, should meet or exceed 80% to ensure effective surveillance. 23. Gender equality and equity must be prioritized in all aspects of polio eradication efforts, with a focus on addressing the unique needs and challenges faced by women, men, and gender-diverse individuals.
